narrative:
Your application was reviewed based on an assessment of your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, and the model estimated a 51.8% probability that you would not pass — a narrow but meaningful margin that ultimately led to the rejection of your application. While this is a close call, the decision reflects specific patterns in your academic profile that, taken together, raised enough concern to tip the outcome unfavorably. Understanding exactly which factors drove this result can help you take meaningful steps forward.

The single most influential factor in this decision was your third-year law school grade ranking. Your standing placed you in the 1st decile within your school — meaning you ranked among the lowest-performing students in your class by that point in your studies. Students who successfully passed the bar exam averaged around the 6th decile, so this gap is substantial and was the strongest signal the model used when assessing your application. Third-year performance is particularly telling because it reflects how well a student has consolidated their legal knowledge heading into the bar exam, and your ranking suggested a significant struggle in that critical final stretch.

Your LSAT score of 36 also played a role in the assessment, though it actually worked in your favor. Since the average LSAT among students who passed was 37.27, your score is slightly below that benchmark, yet the model still interpreted it as a modest positive signal — perhaps because it reflects a baseline of analytical aptitude that partially offsets other concerns. Similarly, your undergraduate GPA of 3.40, which is actually above the average of 3.24 for students who passed, also pushed the prediction in a favorable direction, suggesting that your pre-law academic discipline is a genuine strength in your profile.

The challenge is that these two positive factors — your LSAT and undergraduate GPA — were not strong enough to overcome the weight of your third-year academic performance, which dominated the model's assessment. Your family income background as a lower-middle income student is worth acknowledging too: only about 9.4% of students who passed the bar came from a similar income bracket, which may reflect real-world pressures around resources, study materials, or financial stress that can affect academic outcomes. As a full-time student, you made a commitment that the vast majority of successful bar passers also made, so that aspect of your profile aligns well with those who succeed.

Given all of this, the most impactful thing you can do is focus on strengthening your academic standing before reapplying. If you are still in law school or have the opportunity to retake courses or engage in additional bar preparation, prioritizing that improvement in your legal coursework performance would directly address the primary reason for this outcome. Seeking academic support, tutoring, or structured bar prep programs could make a meaningful difference, and your strong undergraduate GPA shows you are capable of performing at a high level when well-supported.
